children: The European Union and the Philippines struck a "substantial" agreement on a free-trade deal, as persistent geopolitical shocks and tariffs underscore the need for diversification.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she reached the agreement with Philippines President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Tuesday, a milestone that followed her visit to the Southeast Asian country three years earlier to re-launch negotiations.

The two sides aim to deepen bilateral trade and investment, calling the move "a clear signal of reinforced engagement" anchored in a shared interest in a rules-based international order.  The deal is now on a path toward formal conclusion in the coming months.

The Brussels-Manila deal aims to deliver new opportunities for businesses--especially small and medium firms--more jobs, and stronger supply chains at a time when resilience has become a strategic priority.

In 2025, the EU was the Philippines' fourth-largest trading partner, accounting for 8.3% of the country's total trade in goods. The Southeast Asian nation's top exports to the trading bloc include electronic products and agricultural goods.
Global economies been ramping up efforts to bolster ties with Asia-Pacific as U.S. trade policy shifts around tariffs underline the need to secure natural resources and fortify alliances.

Earlier this year, the EU inked a landmark agreement with India and has ongoing trade agreement negotiations in various phases with Malaysia and Thailand. An India-New Zealand FTA is due to come into force next month.

Canada, which is in the midst of a tit-for-tat tariff tiff with Washington, is turning to Asia too. Earlier this week, a top Canadian trade official met with his India counterpart in Mumbai to discuss strengthening trade and investment ties.

In a post on X, Canadian Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu said he that after "a successful round of negotiations with India," he was now traveling to the Philippines for the Asean Economic Ministers' Meeting to advance talks on free trade agreements with both the Philippines and the Asean bloc of 11 member states.
In 2025, Canada's bilateral merchandise trade with Asean rose 24% to 52.4 billion Canadian dollars, equivalent to US$37.33 billion.

Trade uncertainty has been a persistent theme in foreign relations this year since a U.S. Supreme Court ruling struck down many of the tariffs the Trump administration had levied on economies last year over trade imbalances. Since then, the government has continued pursuing tariffs via other routes.

Both the EU and Canada have seen tensions flare with Washington since President Trump's return to office. The U.S. and Canada nearly came to a trade agreement in late August, but talks fell apart at the last minute.
